title: Mahershala Ali Says Winning 2 Oscars Won’t Fix “No Roles” Issue in Hollywood Projects
body:
Mahershala Ali, the two‑time Academy Award winner best known for his roles in “Moonlight” and “Green Book,” told a candid story on a recent episode of the “Carmelo Anthony & Kaz” podcast that his Oscars have done little to change the fundamental dynamics of his career. While the accolades have raised his public profile, Ali explained that the industry still offers him a limited pool of characters, leaving him “like everybody else waiting” for meaningful parts to materialize.

The conversation, which aired as part of the sports‑centric show’s foray into broader cultural topics, revealed a stark contrast between the glamour of award‑season headlines and the day‑to‑day reality of a Black actor navigating Hollywood’s casting landscape. Ali said the “vast majority of projects” he encounters simply lack roles that align with his artistic sensibilities, despite his proven box‑office draw and critical acclaim. “It doesn’t matter that I’ve got two Oscars,” he remarked, “because there aren’t many scripts that actually write me in.” His remarks underscore a growing frustration among elite performers who, even after receiving the highest industry honors, still confront systemic gaps in representation and storytelling.

Industry insiders note that Ali’s experience is emblematic of a broader pattern where award recognition does not automatically translate into a surge of diverse, substantive roles. Historically, actors of color have often seen a temporary boost in visibility after a win, yet the underlying scarcity of well‑written parts persists. Casting directors and studio executives have been urged to expand their pipelines, but progress remains uneven. For Ali, whose career has already spanned indie dramas, high‑budget thrillers, and a leading role in the Marvel universe, the challenge lies not in finding work but in finding work that resonates with his creative ambitions.

Ali’s candidness also highlights the tension between commercial viability and artistic integrity. While his involvement in blockbuster franchises like “Spider‑Man: Across the Spider‑Verse” showcases his marketability, he expressed a desire to gravitate toward projects that explore nuanced human experiences, particularly those that foreground Black narratives without relying on stereotypes. “I want to be part of stories that matter, that push culture forward,” he said, adding that the industry’s current output often feels “repetitive” and “limited in scope.” This sentiment echoes calls from other prominent actors and filmmakers for studios to invest in original scripts that reflect a wider array of lived experiences.

The actor’s remarks arrived at a time when Hollywood is under intensified scrutiny for its diversity practices. Recent reports indicate that while the percentage of films featuring lead characters of color has risen modestly, the proportion of those written and directed by people of color remains low. Initiatives such as the Academy’s inclusion standards and various studio diversity pledges aim to address these disparities, yet the pipeline from script development to green‑light decisions still appears clogged. Ali’s perspective suggests that even with formal policies in place, the cultural shift required to produce a steady stream of compelling roles for actors like him is still a work in progress.

Looking ahead, Ali hinted that his next career moves will be guided less by awards and more by the substance of the material offered. He remains open to collaborations with emerging writers and directors who can craft the “complex, layered” characters he seeks. As the conversation wound down, he expressed cautious optimism that the industry’s ongoing dialogues about representation may eventually yield a richer slate of opportunities. For now, the Oscar‑winning actor continues to navigate a landscape where prestige does not guarantee choice, and his willingness to speak openly may itself become a catalyst for the change he hopes to see.
